title: Chinese Companies Have Set Their Sights on the World's Most Profitable Game Company. Is $5 Billion Expensive, or Cheap?
excerpt: Tencent or Alibaba — who will become Supercell's new owner?
body:
Tencent or Alibaba — who will become Supercell's new owner?

If you had to pick the mobile game company that is best in the world at making money, it would be Supercell, without question.

This Finnish studio, founded in 2010, has spent the past few years "printing money": according to [data from Superdata](http://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/2016-05-26-supercell-printing-money-with-clash-games-superdata), in April 2016 two Supercell games, *Clash of Clans* and *Clash Royale*, each brought in more than $100 million.

Everyone will tell you how fast China's mobile game market has grown these past few years, and there is no shortage of examples of how inventive clever Chinese developers have been at making money from in-game payments. But in front of Supercell, even the people who call the shots in China, the world's largest mobile game market, have to concede defeat. Every Chinese game company wants to be Supercell.

And if you can't be Supercell, buy it.

Word online is that Supercell is on sale for as much as $5 billion, and that the buyer is a Chinese company.

## Why Is It Worth $5 Billion?

$5 billion is not a small number. Glu, its elder in the business — a mobile game company founded in 2001 that has done well enough on the strength of celebrity-branded titles — is worth only $300 million on the market.

![The Clash Royale logo](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/2016081614425418keEd3UpWRLnKgq.jpg-w600)

But for Supercell, the price is not high at all.

Last April, SoftBank, which holds 73% of Supercell, [put its value at between $5.5 billion and $11 billion](http://seekingalpha.com/article/3105566-softbank-supercell-could-be-worth-5-billion-to-11-billion), and some commentators called $5.5 billion low. SoftBank paid $1.5 billion in 2013 for 51% of Supercell, then raised its stake to 73% in May 2015.

Investors' faith and that healthy valuation both come down to Supercell's remarkable numbers. In 2012 the company took in only about $100 million; a year later the figure was $892 million. In 2013 the most startling fact about Supercell was that it earned $2.4 million a day — and it had only two games at the time, *Hay Day* and *Clash of Clans*. Three years on, it has added two more games, and revenue has nearly tripled.

![A chart of Supercell's revenue growth](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702173106qsjgdE0vPxoMhFXH.jpg-w600)

The business grows fast; the company itself is far easier to run. It has only about 180 employees. That is a long way from the six people who started it in 2010, but it is still tiny next to other companies that once occupied a similar position: Rovio, another Finnish mobile game company, has cut more than 300 jobs in the past two years alone, and Zynga had over 3,000 employees at its peak.

Those 180 employees have gathered 100 million active users and more than $2.3 billion a year in revenue. Their games sit near the top of the App Store's main charts, and countless players love them.

Plenty of money, fast growth, few people and high efficiency. It is no surprise that a company like this has become the prize everyone in the investment market wants, and no surprise if the final bid comes in above $5 billion. Supercell is worth it.

## Why Does It Make So Much Money?

Behind that string of enviable numbers, Supercell has released a total of four games: *Hay Day*, *Clash of Clans*, *Boom Beach* and *Clash Royale*.

*Clash of Clans* and *Clash Royale* need no introduction; in fame and reach they belong alongside *Grand Theft Auto V* on consoles or *League of Legends* on the PC. Even Supercell's least famous game, *Hay Day* — where you grow crops and raise pigs — is the best in its category. It is the oldest of Supercell's surviving titles, released in June 2012, and nearly four years later it still [sits around No. 25 on the U.S. App Store's top-grossing chart](https://www.appannie.com/apps/ios/app/hay-day/rank-history/#vtype=day&countries=US&start_date=2016-03-04&end_date=2016-06-01&device=iphone&view=grossing&lm=d), in the top three among family games and the top five among simulation games.

![A scene from Hay Day](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702173107wxXfYTIiaoepQvg5.jpg-w600)

There are many reasons Supercell's games succeed, among them:

- The company caught the mobile game boom at exactly the right moment, while its rivals kept shooting themselves in the foot (look at Rovio).
- Supercell's games have no especially novel ideas, but they are fun, and they are perfect for killing time.
- They stick to one field, and they are careful about every product they ship.
- Supercell is willing to spend on advertising, and the ads are pretty good.

Supercell's games are in fact quite similar to each other: cartoonish art, simple controls that are easy to learn. Besides head-to-head play and trading between players, every game has some kind of guild to give players a sense of belonging and help beginners along. The core of the play is strategy, though it changes a great deal from game to game.

The games are full of amusing detail. In *Hay Day*, a hen about to lay wears an unmistakable "I can't hold it in" expression, and a fattened pig looks like a big cheerful lump; both are hard not to laugh at. In *Clash of Clans*, once you upgrade the barracks the food over the fire turns from roast carrots into roast meat, and in *Boom Beach* the crabs and seagulls react when you tap them.

Fun is not only about being entertaining, of course; it is also about being easy to play. Supercell's games make the most of the scraps of time in a player's day. Because most strategy matches need a connection, a round in a Supercell strategy game runs four or five minutes at most. That lowers the bar for where you can play, and squeezes every last minute out of standing in line, waiting for a bus or staring into space.

Beyond the games, Supercell knows how to run a business. It stays inside one narrow field: after its first browser game failed, it made only mobile games, and generally only mobile strategy games. It never went chasing a Disney deal or a merchandise line the way Rovio did. What made that $2.4 million a day so startling in 2013 was not only the size of the number, but that Supercell was the only game company earning that much purely from publishing mobile games.

It is also careful about what it launches. From its first release in 2011 until now, only four of its games have survived; everything else was killed. Supercell is a company willing to shut down its own projects — the shortest-lived, *Pet vs Orc*, lasted a little over a month. Of the 180 employees, the 70 game developers decide which projects live and which die; in the sauna, [over beers, they killed the pinball game *Smash Land*](http://supercell.com/en/our-story/), and convinced everyone why that was worth doing.

![A screenshot from Smash Land](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702173107lchyDEi8pI0NP7te.jpg-w600)

It is good at selling itself, too. Huge marketing budgets are a specialty of Chinese game companies, and Supercell spends just as freely to promote its games. There was the $9 million, one-minute [Super Bowl ad for *Clash of Clans*](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/18842.html); the [$59.8 million in TV advertising](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/20709.html) that ranked second among all game companies in 2015; the [360-degree panoramic game video](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/18919.html). All of it rests on the games being good — otherwise it would only irritate people, like that nightmare of a Chinese ad line, "Your time is very valuable."

With the games and the marketing both taken care of, Supercell can sit back and wait for people to pay. From the basic gems you use to speed things up to the chests you open in batches, none of these payment hooks is fundamentally new, and although the company keeps insisting it is not "Pay to Win," there is no doubt that putting in more money improves your odds of winning. In its newest game, *Clash Royale*, that smell is stronger still.

Players enjoy it anyway. For one thing, Supercell's games are still fun without spending a cent; for another, players throw themselves in even knowing all of the above. A YouTuber named Chief Pat may be [Supercell's single biggest-spending user](http://www.forbes.com/sites/insertcoin/2016/04/01/the-worlds-best-clash-royale-player-has-spent-12k-on-the-game-and-for-good-reason/#1df4b06fdb71). He has given $18,000 to *Clash of Clans*, and $12,000 to *Clash Royale* in the three months after launch — the way he sees it, that is what it takes to guarantee he has spectacular footage to show off in his YouTube videos.

The most frightening thing a game company can do is make you spend money and enjoy it so much that you come back for more. On the PC, Steam managed it. On phones, Supercell has.

![A player's Clash of Clans village](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702173108lT6LfxdnMES3KI4Q.jpg-w600)

## Who Will Buy It?

Talk about mobile game companies that get you to spend money and players tend to think of someone else: Tencent, and that doctored photo of Pony Ma passed around online — think about it, if you don't pay up, will you get any stronger?

On that score there is really no difference between Supercell and Tencent. Set against a paid download like *Monument Valley*, both stand for the other payment model.

As it happens, in the guesswork of the press and the internet, Tencent is also the most likely buyer for Supercell.

First, Tencent has the money. $5 billion or more is beyond most Chinese game companies, but Tencent can manage it. Its revenue last year was $15.841 billion, and its net cash at year-end was over 19.1 billion yuan. Swallowing Supercell in one bite would be no problem.

More important, investing in and buying overseas game companies has long been Tencent's strategy. In the past two years it has made more than a dozen investments of various sizes in mobile gaming abroad, so it clearly knows what it is doing.

If Tencent lands Supercell, the world's highest-earning game company and the world's highest-earning mobile game company become one. Tencent would of course be glad to hold that position, and would gain revenue, development talent and brand strength from the deal. Supercell, in turn, would get hold of the one thing Tencent has in China, the world's biggest mobile game market, that no one can match: distribution. Social platforms like WeChat and QQ, app stores like Yingyongbao, the machinery to run a game across films, comics and other entertainment products, and, at the most basic level, money and technical support.

![Tencent's WeChat and QQ game portals](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702173108if4JVPyrGcuYhSBv.jpg-w600)

Tencent is not the only candidate, though.

Alibaba has also turned up on the shortlists reported by the press. Alibaba naturally lacks Tencent's gaming pedigree, but that does not stop it from having the money. In 2014 it [invested $120 million in the American mobile game company Kabam and took a 10% stake the following year](http://blogs.wsj.com/venturecapital/2014/07/31/alibaba-invests-120m-in-mobile-gaming-co-kabam-at-valuation-more-than-1-billion/); Kabam's best-known game, made with Disney, is *Marvel Contest of Champions*, which has a modest name on the North American top-grossing charts.

But next to Tencent's overseas mobile game portfolio, Alibaba's is not only much smaller — Kabam's founder and CEO is a Chinese American, which means that in a sense the investment gives Alibaba little useful experience to bring into talks with Supercell and SoftBank.

And what would Alibaba do with Supercell once it had it? Without a gaming pedigree, Alibaba probably would not touch Supercell's operations. Unlike Tencent, which can publish a game in China itself after investing in the studio — Glu's *Kim Kardashian: Hollywood*, for instance — Alibaba, having bought Supercell, would have little to do but park it and wait for it to appreciate before selling it on. Which would, in fact, be a perfectly good investment.

Besides deep-pocketed companies like Tencent and Alibaba, there is one more Chinese company tangled up with Supercell: Kunlun Tech.

Kunlun publishes Supercell's games in China. In 2014 it picked up the Android rights to *Boom Beach* in China, then went on to take the Chinese rights to *Hay Day*, *Clash of Clans* and *Clash Royale* — every Supercell game there is. If some other Chinese company buys Supercell, those rights would basically be saying goodbye to Kunlun, which would mean losing a considerable amount of revenue.

In any Supercell deal, Kunlun's biggest problem is money. Its 2015 revenue was only 1.71 billion yuan, down 7.5% from the year before. A partial purchase or a joint bid are both possible, of course. Kunlun has done this before, teaming up with Qihoo 360 to buy the mobile browser Opera for $1.2 billion.

## Tencent or Alibaba — What Are They Actually Buying?

Judged on its ability to make money, Supercell is certainly worth this much. Its price-to-earnings ratio is quite high.

But low valuations are the norm for game companies, because game revenue is unstable and a hit has a life cycle. Every game is different, but the worry about the curve bending downward matters a great deal.

*Clash of Clans* is nearly four years old now, which makes it one of the longest-lived and highest-earning games there is. Nobody knows when it will start to fade. Supercell says it makes games people will play forever, and so far that looks true — but the same Superdata report that noted *Clash of Clans* passing $100 million in monthly revenue also noted that the game's daily take had slipped from more than $5 million to under $4 million.

![World of Warcraft's subscriber numbers over time. At age four, World of Warcraft was at its peak with the Wrath of the Lich King expansion; now it is stuck in a trough. (Image: [Kotaku](http://kotaku.com/why-world-of-warcraft-lost-so-many-subscribers-1702814469))](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702173109xiy9hWCYKZ6qQ8Jw.jpg-w600)

Comparing *World of Warcraft* with *Clash of Clans* may not be quite fair, but it makes a point: never use one game's current numbers to imagine a game company's future. What matters more is that company's ability to ship the next hit — which means the team behind it.

*World of Warcraft*'s numbers have fallen, but Blizzard is doing fine; look at *Overwatch*, which is everywhere at the moment. *Clash of Clans*'s daily revenue has fallen, but Supercell's staff shipped *Clash Royale* at just the right time.

Tencent and Alibaba are not racing to buy Supercell to grab a few games. What they want is Supercell's ability to build them, and its future — which means the people behind it.

And people are the hardest part of any acquisition to handle. [EA has shown us more than enough](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/25013.html) of the miserable fate of a small company bought by a big one. Most of the time the reasons are these: the core team walks out, and the big company's structure destroys the flat, efficient management the small one used to have.

At a company of only 180 people, an acquirer can sway decisions without effort. A smart acquirer would leave Supercell alone. When SoftBank held an outright controlling stake, it barely interfered. Supercell has said that SoftBank is a company that thinks in centuries.

So what happens when the owner is Tencent or Alibaba?

Even Tencent, which usually likes to throw its weight around, would probably let Supercell keep running on its own. After Riot became a wholly owned subsidiary, Tencent's involvement in *League of Legends* went no further than marketing; the game's content and development stayed with Riot.

Add the earlier example of the Glu investment, and the most likely thing to happen after Tencent takes Supercell is that you will see Supercell's games advertised in more places, and see Supercell change publishers in China. At the very most, Tencent might think about running *Clash of Clans* as a content brand: a film, an animated series, merchandise.

Alibaba would change even less about the games. Supercell's greater value to Alibaba is as a gateway to users worldwide. [For an Alibaba pushing hard on globalization and cross-border e-commerce](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/14774.html), the eventual route might be the one *Angry Birds* took: [selling official merchandise](http://finance.sina.com.cn/roll/2016-05-13/doc-ifxsehvu8885528.shtml).

So even after a Chinese company buys it, players need not fear more things to pay for inside the games (there are already plenty). What matters most is that as long as Supercell's core staff keep making games, you need not worry about your *Clash of Clans* clan or your *Clash Royale* filling up with free dragon-slaying swords, just click to claim. If anything, Supercell moving further into China's somewhat warped mobile game market may, through competition, produce a better result.
